title: Hubble and Webb Find 27 Tiny Icy Worlds Beyond Neptune, Clues to the Solar System's Birth
excerpt: NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have identified 27 previously unknown objects beyond Neptune, offering new clues about how the solar system formed
content:
NASA's Hubble and James Webb Space Telescopes have identified 27 previously unknown objects beyond Neptune, offering new clues about how the solar system formed more than 4 billion years ago.

The two telescopes studied these distant, icy bodies — known as trans-Neptunian objects, or TNOs — in what researchers describe as the deepest survey of this population to date. By combining Hubble's visible-light observations with Webb's infrared data, astronomers examined the objects' sizes, colors and orbital characteristics.

One surprising finding: even the smallest objects showed color patterns similar to those of much larger bodies. That suggests they may have preserved characteristics of their original formation despite billions of years of collisions and changes in their orbits.

The research also found that two populations of TNOs, which formed in different regions of the early solar system, have remarkably similar size distributions — a result that could challenge existing models of how the first planetary building blocks developed.

Webb detected objects as small as approximately 5 kilometers across, while the observations also revealed fewer small bodies than some theoretical models predicted. The findings were reported in two studies published in The Astronomical Journal.

Researchers say further observations will help explain why these ancient objects have retained their characteristics — and what their populations reveal about planet formation. For readers here, it is a reminder that the same telescopes rewriting astronomy textbooks are also, this week, the subject of a separate NASA effort to keep Hubble itself flying longer.
